title: Line Kit
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the geometry chapter. An adult sees dots and strokes being drawn, which a pencil and a ruler do perfectly well. What is actually being settled is what the ends of a stroke say: an arrowhead says it carries on, a dot says it stops, and only a stroke that stops at both ends has a length. The printed exercise then asks for two rays in a figure that draws only one, and the second is hidden inside the line: a point on a line is the start of two rays, one going each way, which the chapter never says but its own definition gives.

writeup.why: Put points down and name them, draw straight strokes through them, and let the ends of each stroke say whether it stops or carries on.
writeup.look: A drawing board with a point stamp, a ruler that turns to any slope, a tray of dots and arrowheads, and a tape measure coiled at one corner.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Line Kit' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the points named, the ends capped or the rays named, against what this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each point takes its letter, each end takes its cap or each ray settles in the name strip, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tool column stands at the left of the working area, 140 by 500 at 64,214: the point stamp at its top, 140 by 90, and the letter tray under it at 64,316, the twenty-six capitals in rows of four, a letter already on the board dimmed in the tray so that no letter can name two points. The magnifier rests at the foot of the column, a round glass 120 across at 74,590. The drawing board fills the middle, 780 by 440 at 220,214, on the panel colour. A stamp puts down one vermilion dot, every dot on the board the same small size, and the curve pen joins named points in the order they are tapped with one freehand deep blue curve. The ruler lies across the board and turns about its middle to any slope; laid through two points it draws one straight deep blue stroke through both, and each end of the stroke waits in an open socket for a cap. The cap tray stands at the right, 134 by 180 at 1016,214, holding vermilion dots and deep blue arrowheads: two dots make a line segment, a dot and an arrowhead a ray, and two arrowheads a line, and a stroke with an open socket is never named. The tape is coiled under the cap tray, 134 by 90 at 1016,410, and unrolls in amber along any stroke from its first end: at a dot it stops and reads the length in centimetres, and at an arrowhead it runs on past the edge of the board with its reading left blank. The ray splitter sits under the tape, 134 by 70 at 1016,516, and works only on a point that sits on a line: tapped there, it lights the line from that point one way to its arrowhead, thick in deep blue, and then the other way in sky blue, the second thing set beside the first. The name strip runs along the foot of the board, 780 by 56 at 220,666, and writes each stroke's name as its second cap lands and each ray's name, starting letter first, as the splitter lights it. The magnifier, passed over a point, spreads the grain of the paper apart under the glass while the dot is redrawn at its one small size. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is a word pad of the twenty-six capitals wherever a point, a stroke or a ray is named, with three keys under them reading line, line segment and ray. Wherever a length or a count is asked for it is twelve number keys three across, with a key beside them reading no length, so a line or a ray is answered by press and never with a number. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. A point is one small dot everywhere on this stage and never grows, whatever the magnifier does to the paper round it. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read either way: until its cap lands, an end shows an open socket, and the stroke carries no name.
writeup.finish: The card shows the board the child drew on, every stroke with its caps and its name, and the rays they found lit from the point they tapped.

phases.win: the paper spreads apart under the magnifier while the dot stays one small mark, and the curve runs through every named point in order
phases.does: stamps points, names each one with a capital letter, passes the magnifier over one, then joins them in order with the curve pen
phases.goal: a point marks a position, has no size, and is named by a capital letter
phases.says: Put a point down and give it a name. Look closer. Does it get any bigger?
phases.check: Away from the screen: mark three points on paper, one of them a fat dot, and name each. How big is each point?
phases.feels: the dot can grow as big as the ink likes, and the place it marks never grows at all
phases.hands: Draw a small chalk dot on the board and name it A. Draw a much fatter dot beside it and name it B. Ask which point is bigger, then ask a child to put a fingertip on exactly the place A marks, and on exactly the place B marks. Last, mark six dots across the board, name them in order and join them with one freehand curve.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does the dot show? Second rung, the phase's: does the place grow when the ink does? Third rung: the board is cut to one named point, and the magnifier passes over it before the second point comes back. The letter pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: on paper a dot is the only thing anyone ever sees of a point, so the size of the ink looks like the size of the point.
wrong.move: calls the point drawn as a fat dot the bigger point.
wrong.screen: the magnifier passes over each dot in turn, and under the glass the paper spreads apart while the exact place each dot marks is found at its middle and held there as one small mark. The two places are restamped side by side at the board's one small size, the fat ink left faintly behind the second, and the child's answer stays in the slot with nothing marked.

wrong.why: a letter used across the board looks free once its point is out of sight, and any letter seems to do as a name.
wrong.move: gives a second point the letter already standing on the first, so one letter names two places.
wrong.screen: the letter tray holds that capital dimmed, and the two points the child meant to share it are lit one after the other while the dimmed letter pulses. A free capital is offered beside the second point, and the child's name stays written in the strip beside it until another is chosen.

phases.screen: an empty drawing board with the point stamp, the letter tray and the magnifier waiting
phases.soWhat: A point marks a place and has no size. It is shown by a dot and named by a capital letter.

phases.win: the tape runs off both edges of the board without finding an end, and the line is named by its two points
phases.does: draws a straight stroke through both points, caps both ends with arrowheads, turns the ruler to draw lines across, upright and slanting, then runs the tape along one
phases.goal: a line is straight, has an arrowhead at each end, and has no length that can be measured
phases.says: Draw it straight through both points. Now run the tape along it. Where does it stop?
phases.check: Draw one line across, one upright and one slanting, and name each by two points on it. How many arrowheads did you draw?
phases.feels: the arrowheads are not where the line ends, they are the line saying it does not end
phases.hands: Stretch a string across the room and tape a card arrowhead to each end. Ask where the line stops. Then mark C and D on the board, lay a ruler through them and draw one straight stroke with an arrowhead at each end. Draw a line across, one upright and one slanting, and ask how long each one is.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is at each end of the stroke? Second rung, the phase's: where does the tape stop? Third rung: the board is cut to one line across, and the tape runs along it before the upright and slanting lines come back. The letter pad and the no length key stay open.

wrong.why: a stroke on paper has to stop somewhere, and a dot is the tidy way to finish a stroke off.
wrong.move: caps a line with a dot at each end, so what was meant to be line CD is drawn as a stroke that stops.
wrong.screen: the name strip writes line segment under the stroke, not line, and the tape runs along it and stops at the second dot with a reading. Beside it the ruler draws the same stroke again with an arrowhead at each end, and the tape along that one runs off both edges of the board with its reading blank. Both strokes stay drawn with their names under them, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the drawn part of a line is a definite size on the paper, and a ruler laid against it gives a number as readily as it does for anything else.
wrong.move: measures from one arrowhead to the other and gives that as the length of the line.
wrong.screen: the tape is laid from arrowhead to arrowhead and keeps unrolling past each one, the board sliding to show the line carrying on beyond where it was drawn, while the reading stays blank. The child's number stays in the slot, and the key reading no length is lit on the pad beside it.

phases.screen: two named points on the board with the ruler lying across them and both end caps waiting
phases.soWhat: A line is straight, has an arrowhead at each end and no end points, and has no length that can be measured.
phases.concept: A line goes on for ever both ways

phases.win: the tape stops at the second dot of the segment and reads its length, and on the ray it unrolls off the board
phases.does: runs the tape along each stroke and reads the one length it finds
phases.goal: a line segment has two end points and a length, and a ray has one end point and goes on in one direction
phases.says: Which one can the tape measure? Why does the other one run away?
phases.check: A stroke has a dot at one end and an arrowhead at the other. Name it from the right end. Can a ruler measure it?
phases.feels: a dot says stop and an arrowhead says keep going, and the tape believes them both
phases.hands: Cut one piece of string with a knot at each end, and leave a second piece knotted at one end and still joined to the ball at the other. Ask which one can be laid along a ruler and read. Then draw segment GH and ray MN on the board and let the class say why only one of them has a length.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many dots does the stroke have? Second rung, the phase's: at which end does the tape stop? Third rung: the board is cut to one segment, and one of its dots is swapped for an arrowhead while the tape runs along it. The letter pad and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: the part of the ray drawn on the paper is short and plainly starts and stops on the page, so it looks as measurable as the segment beside it.
wrong.move: gives ray MN a length, reading the ruler from M to the arrowhead.
wrong.screen: the tape unrolls from the dot at M, passes N and reaches the arrowhead, and keeps on unrolling past it off the board with its reading blank. The segment beside it is measured again and its tape stops at the second dot with a number. The child's length stays in the slot beside the no length key, nothing marked.

wrong.why: a segment can be named from either end, GH or HG, so the order of the letters seems not to matter for a ray either.
wrong.move: names the ray from its arrowhead end, writing ray NM for the ray that starts at M.
wrong.screen: the splitter draws the ray the child's name describes, starting at N and running back through M and on past it in sky blue, a different ray pointing the other way. The drawn ray stays lit starting at M, the two stand side by side with their names under them, and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: two strokes side by side, one capped with a dot at each end and one with a dot and an arrowhead
phases.soWhat: A line segment has two end points and can be measured; a ray has one end point, goes on in one direction and cannot be measured.
phases.concept: A segment has two ends, a ray has one

phases.win: the line lights one way and then the other from the tapped point, and three ray names settle, each starting with its letter
phases.does: taps the middle point, watches the splitter light each way in turn, and names every ray that starts there
phases.goal: a point on a line is the start of two rays, one going each way, each named from that point first
phases.says: Tap the middle point. How many rays start here? Name each one from this point.
phases.check: Mark A, B and C in that order on a line. Name the two rays that start at B.
phases.feels: a point on a line has the line running away from it both ways, and each way is a ray of its own
phases.hands: Stretch a string line across the room and stand a child on it. Ask how many ways they could walk off along the string from where they stand without turning. Two. Tape a card arrow to each end and say that each walk is a ray starting where the child stands. Then mark three points on a drawn line and ask for the rays that start at the middle one.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which point do the rays start at? Second rung, the phase's: which ways can you go along the line from there? Third rung: the board is cut to a line through two points with a third marked between them, and the splitter lights one way before the child names the other. The letter pad stays open.

wrong.why: every ray shown so far was drawn as a separate stroke, so a ray hidden inside a line does not look like a ray at all.
wrong.move: names only ray LP, the one drawn as a stroke of its own, and says there is no second ray to find.
wrong.screen: the splitter lights the line from L one way, out through M to its arrowhead, and holds it lit beside the drawn ray, then lights the other way through K in sky blue. The names ray LM and ray LK write themselves into the strip under the child's one name, which stays where it was written, and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a line is named by two of its points in either order, and a ray along the line looks as though it should be named the same way.
wrong.move: names the two rays along the line with the starting point last, writing ray KL and ray ML.
wrong.screen: the splitter draws the rays the child's names describe, one starting at K and one starting at M, each in sky blue and each running on through L. The two rays that start at L are lit beside them in deep blue, all four names stand in the strip, and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: a line through three named points, with a fourth point off the line joined to the middle one as a ray
phases.soWhat: A point on a line is the start of two rays, one going each way, and each is named from that point first.
phases.concept: Two rays start at every point on a line

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the middle point is tapped. The line lights from that point one way, out through the next letter to the arrowhead at the edge, and holds; then it lights the other way in sky blue and holds too, so the one line is seen as two rays pointing apart from one dot. Their names write themselves into the strip, each beginning with the tapped letter, beside the name of the ray that was drawn all along. The tap can be made on any point of the line as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the board is empty, the point stamp stands at its left with the letter tray open under it, and the magnifier rests at the foot of the tool column. On the second two named points stand on the board with the ruler lying across them and both end sockets of the stroke open and empty. On the third two strokes lie one above the other, one capped with a dot at each end and one with a dot and an arrowhead, with the tape coiled at the left hand end of each. On the fourth a line runs across the board through three named points, a fourth point off the line is joined to the middle one as a ray, and the ray splitter waits beside the middle point. The running count at the top left holds what has been named or capped against what this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the point stamp, or an empty socket, or the coiled tape, or the middle point, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the end of a stroke says. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number of points and strokes with any caps, and the tape, the magnifier and the ray splitter open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on points having no size, lines drawn three ways with an arrowhead at each end, telling a segment from a ray, and naming the rays that start at a point on a line.
voiceLines: An empty board, a point stamp and a ruler. What does the end of a stroke tell you?
Put a point down and give it a name. Look closer. Does it get any bigger?
Draw it straight through both points. Now run the tape along it. Where does it stop?
Which one can the tape measure? Why does the other one run away?
Tap the middle point. How many rays start here? Name each one from this point.
A new board. Look at both ends before you name anything.
Free play. Any points, any strokes, any caps, with the tape and the ray splitter open.
Run the tape along it again, and read what each end says.
Every point named, every end capped, and both rays found where only one was drawn.

observations.why: The dot only shows where the point is, and a place has no length and no breadth to grow.
observations.soWhat: A point has no size. A bigger dot is a bigger mark of ink, not a bigger point.
observations.observe: The paper spread apart under the magnifier and the dot stayed one small mark.

observations.why: An arrowhead says the stroke carries on, and something that carries on for ever has no end for the tape to stop at.
observations.soWhat: A line has no end points and no length that can be measured.
observations.observe: The tape ran off both edges of the board along the line and never gave a reading.

observations.why: The segment stopped at both its dots, and the ray stops only at its one end point.
observations.soWhat: A segment can be measured. A ray starts at an end point, goes on in one direction and cannot be measured.
observations.observe: Swapping one dot for an arrowhead took the reading off the tape.

observations.why: A point on a line has the line running away from it both ways, and each way is a ray that starts at that point.
observations.soWhat: A point on a line is the start of two rays, one each way, and each is named from that point first.
observations.observe: The splitter lit two rays from a point where only one ray had been drawn.

description: Stamp points, draw straight strokes through them, cap every end with a dot or an arrowhead, and find the two rays that start at a point on a line.

serves.exercise: drawing three horizontal, three vertical and one slanting straight line
joining six named points in order with curved lines

source_tool.description: A drawing board fills the stage with a point stamp, a ruler that turns to any slope, and a tray of end caps holding dots and arrowheads. A point is stamped with one tap and named from a tray of capital letters, and no letter can be given to two points on one board. A magnifier passes over any point and spreads the paper under it apart while the dot stays one small mark, because a point marks a place and has no size. A curve pen joins named points in order with freehand curves. The ruler draws a straight stroke through two points, and each end of the stroke waits for a cap: two dots make a line segment, a dot and an arrowhead make a ray, and two arrowheads make a line. A measuring tape runs along whatever has been drawn. On a segment it stops at the second dot and reads a length; on a ray or a line it keeps unrolling off the edge of the board and never finds an end. A ray splitter works on any point that sits on a line: tapped, it lights the line one way from the point and then the other way, and names each ray from the tapped point first.
source_tool.art_direction: A drawing board with ruler and caps / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.note: THERE IS NO MODE AXIS ON THIS TOOL FAMILY. learn, practice and freeplay are gone and are not replaced by three of anything else: the axis itself is wrong for a tool a child works alone. See phase_mount.

authored.freeplay: Free Play. Any number of points and strokes with any caps, and the tape, the magnifier and the ray splitter open.
authored.practice: Practice, child alone. Eight items on points having no size, lines drawn three ways with an arrowhead at each end, telling a segment from a ray, and naming the rays that start at a point.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a drawing board with a ruler and a point stamp, a tracing finger and a flag, a walker and a string, square tiles on squared paper, a pair of compasses with a metal point and a pencil arm, a sheet of paper that folds, an upright mirror, solids on a turntable, flat nets that fold up, hinged arms, a clock face and a grid of pictures.

A line is always drawn with an arrowhead at each end, a ray with a dot at its end point and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read as either.

A point is drawn as one small dot of one size wherever it appears, named by a capital letter beside it. Within one figure no letter ever names two different things, and a figure never renames a part it has already named.

Every labelled length is one the figure could really have, and every figure is drawn to scale with its labels. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five, and a stepped shape's sides close up exactly.
A figure on squared paper sits exactly on the grid lines, with every side along a line and every square either wholly inside it or wholly outside it.

A circle drawn to show its parts has its centre marked as a dot and named. Every radius is drawn from that dot to the curve, and a diameter always passes exactly through the dot. A circle that is a view of a solid carries a dot only where the solid has a point, so a cylinder seen from above is a plain circle.
A right angle carries a small square corner mark, and every other angle an arc drawn close to its vertex between the arms.

A line of symmetry and a mirror line are drawn dotted and lie exactly where the fold falls. A fold line being tried is drawn solid and turns dotted only once the fold is kept. Every mirror line stands upright unless the frame says it lies across, and an image sits exactly as far behind the line as the thing in front of it, turned the other way round.
A solid is drawn with its hidden edges dashed. Views of one solid are drawn at one scale, so the front view and the side view of a box are exactly the same height.

Clock hands point exactly at the numbers and the minute hand is the longer. Where the angle between the hands is shown, both angles are shaded and the smaller one is outlined. No clock is set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock.
A grid carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, and each picture in it appears once.
A shape, a side or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a line, a point, a square or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that opens on the point cannot afford a frame where a point has to be hunted for. A length being measured, walked, added or named, the tape, the walker's sum, a radius being measured, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted, so a dotted line always means a true line of symmetry. Sky blue is the second thing set beside the first: a fold being tried, drawn solid until it is kept, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter, and the larger angle between clock hands. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because a point is a round dot, a measured length carries its number, a line of symmetry is dotted, a fold being tried is solid and a hidden edge is dashed.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Run the tape along it again, and read what each end says.
voice.onNext: A new board. Look at both ends before you name anything.
voice.opening: An empty board, a point stamp and a ruler. What does the end of a stroke tell you?
voice.onFinish: Every point named, every end capped, and both rays found where only one was drawn.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any points, any strokes, any caps, with the tape and the ray splitter open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A line goes on for ever both ways
A segment has two ends, a ray has one
Two rays start at every point on a line

placement.where: After string has been stretched across the room with card arrows taped to its ends, and cut into a piece with two knots and a piece with a knot and an arrow. The tool is what runs a tape along a ray and lets it keep unrolling, which a ruler on paper cannot show.

answer_key.rule: A point marks a position and has no size. It is shown by a dot and named by a capital letter. A line is straight, goes on for ever in both directions, is drawn with an arrowhead at each end and has no length that can be measured; it is named by any two points on it, and it can run across, upright or slanting. A line segment is part of a line with two end points and a length that can be measured. A ray starts at one end point and goes on for ever in one direction, so it cannot be measured, and it is named from its end point first. A point on a line is the start of two rays, one going each way along the line.
answer_key.wrong: The tape is run along the stroke again at walking pace, and the cap at each end is lit in turn while its meaning is said. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A point marks a place, and a dot is just the way that place is shown on paper.
The glass makes the ink look bigger, but the place it marks has not moved or grown.
So point R still has no length and no breadth, and it keeps its capital letter name.
items.answer: No. Point R has no size at all; the dot only shows where it is
items.question: A dot is drawn on a card and named R. Seen through a magnifying glass, the dot looks bigger. Has point R grown?
items.checkpoint: A point has no size; a dot shows where it is, and a capital letter names it.
items.misconception: Thinking a bigger dot is a bigger point, or naming a point with a small letter or a number.

steps: The stroke is straight and passes through C and D, so it is named by those two points.
An arrowhead at each end says it carries on past the edge in both directions.
Something with no end cannot be measured, so line CD has no fixed length.
items.answer: It is line CD, and it has no length that can be measured, because it goes on for ever both ways
items.question: Points C and D are marked on a board. A straight stroke passes through both and has an arrowhead at each end. What is it, and how long is it?
items.checkpoint: A line has an arrowhead at each end, no end points, and no length that can be measured.
items.misconception: Measuring from one arrowhead to the other and giving that as the length of the line.

steps: A ruler measures from one end to the other, so the stroke needs two ends.
Segment GH stops at G and at H, so it has a length that can be measured.
Ray MN stops only at M; its arrowhead says it carries on for ever, so it has no length.
items.answer: Segment GH, because it has two end points. Ray MN starts at M and goes on for ever beyond N
items.question: Segment GH has a dot at G and a dot at H. Ray MN has a dot at M and an arrowhead beyond N. Which of them can be measured with a ruler?
items.checkpoint: A segment has two end points and a length; a ray has one end point and goes on in one direction.
items.misconception: Calling a ray measurable because the part drawn on the page looks short.

steps: F sits on the line between E and G.
From F the line goes on one way through E and the other way through G, so two rays start at F.
A ray is named from its end point first, so they are ray FE and ray FG.
items.answer: Ray FE and ray FG, one going each way from F
items.question: Points E, F and G lie in that order on a line with an arrowhead at each end. Name the two rays that start at F along the line.
items.checkpoint: A point on a line is the start of two rays, one each way, even when neither is drawn on its own.
items.misconception: Finding only one ray because only one was drawn separately, or naming a ray with its end point last.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Five dots are drawn in a row. Name them with capital letters, then join them in order with a curved line. How many curved pieces join one dot to the next?
items.final_answer: Four. With the dots named A, B, C, D and E, the pieces go from A to B, B to C, C to D and D to E

items.question: One point is drawn as a tiny dot and another as a big dot. Which point is bigger?
items.final_answer: Neither. A point has no size, so both dots only mark a place

items.question: Draw four horizontal lines, two vertical lines and two slanting lines. How many arrowheads do you draw altogether?
items.final_answer: Sixteen, because each of the eight lines has an arrowhead at both ends

items.question: Line UV is drawn standing straight up the page. Is it horizontal, vertical or slanting, and what is its length?
items.final_answer: It is vertical, and it has no length that can be given, because a line goes on for ever both ways

items.question: A stroke has a dot at one end and an arrowhead at the other. Is it a line, a line segment or a ray?
items.final_answer: A ray, because it has one end point and goes on in one direction

items.question: Segment JK is six centimetres long. The dot at K is swapped for an arrowhead. Can it still be measured?
items.final_answer: No. It is now ray JK, which starts at J and goes on for ever beyond K

items.question: Points A, B, C and D lie in that order on a line. Name the two rays that start at C along the line.
items.final_answer: Ray CB, which carries on through A, and ray CD, going the other way

items.question: A line passes through K, L and M in that order. A ray starts at L and passes through P, which is not on the line. Name three rays that start at L.
items.final_answer: Ray LP, which is drawn, and ray LK and ray LM along the line, one going each way

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: puts a point down with one tap
names a point with a capital letter, never the same letter twice on one board
spreads the paper under a point apart while the dot stays one small mark
joins named points in order with freehand curves
draws a straight stroke through two points, turned to any slope
puts a dot or an arrowhead on each end of a stroke
measures along a stroke, stopping at a dot and running off at an arrowhead
lights the two rays that start at a tapped point on a line

teaching_notes: Draw with a real ruler and a sharp pencil before the tool is opened, and make the class say what each end of every stroke means. An arrowhead says it carries on, and a dot says it stops. Two sentences on the page need care. It calls a point the smallest shape in geometry; say instead that a point has no size at all, which its own next sentence says. It says a line runs usually along a straight path and then that a line always means a straight one; keep the second, and leave out its example of a road, whose two edges are two separate things, each with ends, and so not a line at all. The exercise then asks for two rays in a figure that draws only one. Before anyone hunts for a second drawn ray, stand a child on a string line and ask how many ways they could walk off along it without turning. Two, so a point on a line is the start of two rays. Name every ray from its end point first, and let the class hear that ray FE and ray EF are not the same ray.
generation_prompt: Build a drawing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A drawing board fills the working area with a point stamp, a ruler that turns to any slope, and a tray of end caps holding dots and arrowheads. A point is stamped with one tap and named from a tray of capital letters; a letter already on the board is dimmed in the tray, so no letter names two points. A magnifier passing over a point spreads the paper under it apart while the dot is redrawn at the same small size. A curve pen joins named points in the order they are tapped with smooth freehand curves. The ruler draws a straight stroke through two points, and each end of the stroke waits for a cap, a dot or an arrowhead. A measuring tape runs along any stroke; it stops at a dot and reads the length in centimetres, and at an arrowhead it keeps unrolling past the edge of the board with no reading. A ray splitter, used on a point that sits on a line, lights the line from that point one way and then the other and writes each ray's name starting with the tapped point. Every line is drawn with an arrowhead at each end, every ray with a dot and one arrowhead, and every segment with a dot at each end. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Stamp a point and give it a capital letter. Draw a straight stroke with the ruler. Cap each end with a dot or an arrowhead. Run the tape along it. Tap a point on a line to find its two rays.
